questions.prompt: How do reflective roofs reduce warming?

choices.A: They store rainwater beneath buildings.
choices.B: They send more sunlight away instead of absorbing it.
choices.C: They create shade with tall plants.
choices.D: They release heat only at night.

questions.correctAnswer: They send more sunlight away instead of absorbing it.
questions.explanation: The passage directly explains that reflective surfaces absorb less sunlight.
questions.stimulusText:
On sunny days, dark roofs and pavement absorb energy and release it as heat. In neighborhoods with few trees, this process can make outdoor temperatures noticeably higher than in nearby areas with more vegetation. City planners use several strategies to reduce this local warming.
One strategy is to install reflective roofs. Their light-colored or specially coated surfaces send more sunlight away instead of absorbing it. Another approach adds plants to rooftops. These green roofs provide shade, and water evaporating from their soil and leaves helps cool the surrounding air. Street trees can offer similar benefits while also shading sidewalks and building walls.
No single method works best everywhere. A green roof is heavier than a conventional roof and may require structural reinforcement. Trees need room for roots and years to mature. Reflective coatings are comparatively quick to apply, but they do not create habitat or capture rainwater as planted roofs can.
For this reason, planners first examine a block's buildings, available space, rainfall, and budget. A combination—perhaps reflective roofs on warehouses and trees beside homes—often provides greater benefits than repeating one solution throughout an entire neighborhood.

questions.prompt: Why may a subway map bend geographic accuracy?

choices.A: To hide stations from travelers
choices.C: To make route connections easier to understand
choices.D: To copy the shape of a highway map

questions.correctAnswer: To make route connections easier to understand
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that simplified geography can clarify connections.
questions.stimulusText:
A map appears to offer certainty. Lines define roads, colors separate land from water, and symbols promise that important places can be reduced to a tidy key. Yet every map is also a collection of choices. Its maker decides what to include, what to simplify, and what scale will serve the map's purpose.
A subway map, for example, may bend geography so riders can understand connections quickly. A hiking map emphasizes elevation and water sources, details that a highway map may omit. Neither map is dishonest because it leaves something out. Each becomes useful by refusing to show everything.
This selectiveness carries a responsibility. If a map intended for emergency planning omits a small bridge, the absence may matter greatly. Likewise, an old map can reveal the priorities of its time through the names and borders it displays. Readers should therefore ask not only, “What does this map show?” but also, “Who made it, for whom, and why?”
Maps guide us best when we treat them neither as perfect mirrors nor as mere decorations. They are arguments made with distance and direction—powerful precisely because they turn a crowded world into a pattern we can examine.

choices.C: electricity
choices.D: air pressure

questions.correctAnswer: gravity
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the heavier droplets downward.
questions.stimulusText:
In some dry coastal regions, mist arrives even when rain is scarce. Mist consists of tiny water droplets suspended in air. A dew screen captures some of those droplets as wind carries them through a mesh panel.
When droplets strike the mesh, they join with other droplets and grow heavier. Gravity pulls the water downward into a channel, which directs it toward a storage tank. The mesh must allow air to pass while providing enough surface for droplets to collect. A solid wall would force much of the moving air around it.
Dew screens do not create water, and their output varies. Wind speed, droplet size, mesh design, and the number of misty hours all affect collection. The stored water may also require treatment, depending on how it will be used and what substances are present in the air or on the equipment.
Because performance depends on local conditions, planners test small collectors before installing a large system. Where mist is frequent and other water sources are limited, nets can supplement rather than replace existing supplies.

Street names can preserve clues about landscape, language, and human history. A name may describe a physical feature, honor a person, recall an event, or carry forward a word from an earlier language. Yet names that seem permanent often have complicated histories.
The same road or square may have been known by several communities, each using a different name. Municipal clerks sometimes selected one version for official documents, while local speakers continued using another. Spellings also changed when sounds from one language were represented in the alphabet of another.

Comparing sources helps researchers distinguish strong evidence from an appealing guess.

questions.stimulusText:
A seed may appear inactive, yet it contains a living embryo and stored food. Many seeds begin growing soon after receiving water, oxygen, and a suitable temperature. Others remain dormant even when these basic conditions are present. Dormancy prevents growth until additional signals suggest that survival is likely.
Different species use different signals. Some seeds have coats so hard that water cannot enter until weathering, soil movement, or an animal’s digestion weakens the covering. Certain forest plants respond to chemicals in smoke or to heat from a fire. Because fire removes dense vegetation, a seed that sprouts afterward may encounter more sunlight and less competition. Other seeds require weeks of cold before they can germinate. This delay keeps them from sprouting during a brief warm period in autumn, when young plants might soon be killed by winter.
Dormancy also spreads risk over time. Seeds from one plant may not all awaken during the same season. If drought destroys one year’s seedlings, seeds still resting in the soil may grow under better conditions later. For farmers and gardeners, dormancy can be inconvenient, but understanding its triggers allows them to imitate nature—scratching a hard coat, chilling seeds, or applying carefully controlled heat.

For farmers and gardeners, dormancy can be inconvenient, but understanding its triggers allows them to imitate nature—scratching a hard coat, chilling seeds, or applying carefully controlled heat.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what resource does the tree provide to the fungi?

choices.A: Sunlight
choices.C: Phosphorus
choices.D: Oxygen

questions.correctAnswer: Sugar
questions.explanation: The passage states that trees make sugars and pass some of that resource to fungi through their roots.
questions.stimulusText:
On a tree's roots, certain fungi form threadlike networks called mycorrhizae. These fungi do not merely grow beside the roots; they establish a partnership with the tree. The fungal threads extend far into the surrounding soil, reaching spaces too narrow for most roots. From those spaces, the fungi absorb water and minerals, especially phosphorus, and pass some of these resources to the tree.
The exchange also benefits the fungi. Trees use sunlight to produce sugars through photosynthesis. Some of that sugar travels to the roots and then to the fungi, which cannot make their own food from sunlight. Both partners therefore gain something difficult to obtain alone.
Researchers once described these networks mainly as underground pipelines connecting plants. That comparison can be useful, but it is incomplete. Soil conditions, fungal species, and the health of individual trees all affect what moves through a network. Furthermore, fungi use much of the sugar they receive for their own growth. The relationship is cooperation, not a system in which one organism simply serves another.
Scientists study these partnerships by tracing substances marked with special, detectable forms of elements. Such studies reveal movement through roots and fungi without requiring researchers to dig up and destroy the entire network.

questions.prompt: What later evidence supported Tharp's interpretation of the central valley?

choices.A: New photographs of the ocean surface
choices.C: Changes in ship design
choices.D: Earthquake locations aligned with the valley

questions.correctAnswer: Earthquake locations aligned with the valley
questions.explanation: The passage directly states that independently plotted earthquake locations lined up with the central valley.
questions.stimulusText:
In the early 1900s, ocean charts could still contain large blank areas. Marie Tharp, born in 1920, would later help transform those blanks into a detailed picture of the seafloor. Working with thousands of depth measurements collected by research ships, she plotted each number by hand along the ships' routes. The task demanded patience: a single voyage could produce long rolls of data, and the measurements formed only narrow paths across a vast ocean.
Tharp compared one route with another, using the scattered lines to infer the landscape between them. Her maps revealed mountain chains, plains, and a deep central valley running through the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At first, some colleagues doubted the valley because it supported the then-controversial idea that Earth's crust moves. Tharp checked the data rather than removing the feature.
Later, earthquake locations plotted by another researcher lined up with the valley. This independent evidence strengthened the interpretation. When Tharp's seafloor maps were eventually published for broad audiences, they allowed people to see the ocean bottom not as a smooth basin but as a varied landscape.
Her achievement did not come from traveling to every mapped location. It came from recognizing a coherent pattern in measurements gathered by many expeditions—and from trusting careful analysis when an unexpected picture emerged.
